title: Tang Dynasty Bronze Mirror
intro: This is a bronze mirror, cast in China about twelve hundred years ago. The side facing you is the decorated back. The other side was polished until it reflected.
materials: High-tin bronze, cast in a two-piece mould
provenance: Excavated from a tomb near Xi'an, Shaanxi province, in 1955. Held in a museum collection since 1961.
facts: The polished face was the working mirror. The decorated side faced away from the user.
The design shows lions among grapevines, a motif that arrived in China along the Silk Road from Central Asia and Persia.
The high tin content made the polished surface unusually bright and silvery, but it also made the metal brittle and easy to crack.
Mirrors like this were often placed in tombs, where they were believed to protect the dead and light the way.
The central boss has a hole through it, so a silk cord could be threaded and the mirror hung or carried.
Tang mirrors were frequently given as imperial gifts, and some carry inscriptions naming an occasion.
unknown: The specific workshop that cast this mirror is not recorded, nor the name of its owner. Whether the lion motif carried a protective meaning in China, or was purely decorative, is still debated by scholars.
